opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, because the bottlenecks for this class of model are pretty different from what people are used to with language models.

The big one is the pair representation. In an AlphaFold-style architecture like Chai-1, you're not just keeping a sequence of token embeddings. You're keeping an N-by-N representation of every pair of residues or atoms-level tokens. Then the trunk runs operations like triangle multiplicative updates and triangle attention over it, which scale roughly cubically in the number of tokens. So memory and compute blow up fast as complexes get bigger. A single protein of a few hundred residues is fine. Once you get into large multimers, antibody–antigen complexes with ligands, or nucleic acids, you hit the wall quickly.

That shapes everything. In training, you can't feed full structures, so you crop to a fixed number of tokens. The crop size becomes a real modeling decision, not just an engineering one, because it determines what long-range context the model ever sees. Pushing that crop size up through memory optimizations directly affects model quality.

At inference you don't get to crop. People want to fold the whole thing. So a lot of the work is making the trunk fit and run: chunking the triangle operations so you never materialize the full intermediate tensors, fusing kernels so you're not bouncing activations in and out of high-bandwidth memory, using lower precision where it's numerically safe, and being careful about which layers truly need to be in fp32. Some of these ops are surprisingly sensitive, so you can't blindly cast everything to bf16.

Then there's the diffusion module on top. Generating a structure means running the denoiser for many steps, and often you want several samples per input so you can rank them. The trunk runs once, or a few times with recycling, but the diffusion head runs a lot. So you think about amortizing: cache the trunk outputs and make the per-step denoiser as cheap as possible.

And there's the stuff that's easy to forget: featurization, MSA and template search if you're using them, and data loading. For a while the homology search could take longer than the neural network itself. That's part of why we cared about the model working well in single-sequence mode or with language-model embeddings instead of MSAs. It isn't just about accuracy. It changes the whole cost profile of running the thing at scale.

So zooming out, the reason engineering matters so much is that the compute budget directly limits what you can train on and what users can run. If you can make the model two or three times more memory-efficient, that's not just a cost saving. It means bigger crops in training, bigger complexes at inference, more samples for ranking, and ultimately better science coming out the other end.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing people sometimes miss about a Chai 1-style model is that it's not a language model in terms of its compute profile. In a transformer LLM, almost everything is big matrix multiplies, which is exactly what GPUs are built for, and the whole optimization story is about memory bandwidth and KV caches. A structure model like Chai 1 or AlphaFold 3 looks very different. The core of it is a trunk operating on pair representations, so you have an N by N by channel tensor where N is the number of tokens, which for us means residues plus ligand atoms and so on. Then on top of that you have triangle attention and triangle multiplicative updates, which are cubic in N. So the moment you go from a 300-residue protein to a 1,500-token complex with a few ligands and some nucleic acid, your compute and your memory don't scale gently, they explode.

So the bottlenecks are really two things. One is raw memory. Those pair activations are enormous, and if you're training with gradients you need to hold a lot of them, so you end up doing a lot of activation checkpointing and being very careful about what lives in HBM at any moment. The other is that a lot of these ops are kind of awkward. Triangle attention isn't a standard attention pattern, so out of the box you don't get FlashAttention for free, and the naive implementation materializes huge intermediate tensors and spends its time moving memory around rather than doing math. We spent real effort on fused kernels for those pieces, and that's where a lot of the practical wins came from.

And then the diffusion head adds its own flavor. During training you're sampling many noise levels per structure and running the diffusion module repeatedly, so even though it's cheaper per step than the trunk, you're doing it a lot of times, and at inference you're doing multiple samples with many denoising steps. So the trunk is the heavy thing you want to run once and cache, and the diffusion module is the thing you want to make really fast per call.

The honest framing is that the biology constrains the architecture, and the architecture is just not a natural fit for the hardware the way LLMs are. So engineering optimization isn't a nice-to-have, it's what decides whether you can train on long complexes at all, and whether people can actually run the model on a single GPU rather than needing a whole node for one prediction.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in terms of how quickly you can run the experiment loop. You have a fixed compute budget, and you’re making choices about how large a model to train, how much data to show it, and how many different ideas you can try. If an engineering optimization makes training twice as fast, you can spend that on a bigger run, but you can also spend it on more experiments. That second effect can be really important.

For a Chai 1-type model, you’re also dealing with representations of relationships between atoms or residues. Those can grow quadratically with the size of the input, so memory becomes a bottleneck alongside raw computation. You can have plenty of arithmetic capacity on the GPU and still spend a lot of time moving tensors around or materializing intermediate results.

So the engineering work is about figuring out what’s actually limiting you: memory traffic, expensive operations, communication between GPUs, or something in the input pipeline. Then you optimize that bottleneck. The payoff is that you can test scientific ideas that would otherwise be too expensive, or take too long to get an answer on.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it in terms of iteration speed. If you have a fixed compute budget, making a training step faster means you can run more experiments, and that can matter as much as making any one run bigger.

For a Chai-1-type model, you’re working with representations of atoms and pairs of residues, so some of those tensors get large very quickly as the size of the system increases. That puts pressure on both compute and memory. You can have plenty of theoretical FLOPs available and still spend a lot of time moving data around or materializing intermediate tensors.

So the engineering question is: where is the time actually going? Can you fuse operations, avoid storing an intermediate, or distribute the work more efficiently? And then at inference, if you’re generating multiple candidate structures, the cost of each sample matters too. Those optimizations translate into more experiments during development and more predictions people can actually afford to run.
